Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১) Which is not a cardinal sign of inflammation?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
The five cardinal signs of inflammation are rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling), dolor (pain), and functio laesa (loss of function). Rubor and calor result from arteriolar vasodilation and increased blood flow. Tumor is caused by increased vascular permeability leading to edema, while dolor results from inflammatory mediators such as bradykinin and prostaglandins, along with pressure from edema. Pallor (paleness) is not a cardinal sign of inflammation; it is more commonly associated with vasoconstriction, anemia, or reduced blood flow.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Five cardinal signs of inflammation:

    • Rubor – Redness

    • Calor – Heat

    • Tumor – Swelling

    • Dolor – Pain

    • Functio laesa – Loss of function

  • Histamine and nitric oxide contribute to vasodilation.

  • Bradykinin and PGE₂ are major mediators of inflammatory pain.

Exam Pearl:
Remember the classic five signs of inflammation: Rubor, Calor, Tumor, Dolor, and Functio laesa—Pallor is not one of them.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ২) Which is not a feature of acute inflammation?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Acute inflammation is characterized by rapid onset, short duration (minutes to days), and predominance of neutrophils. It typically produces prominent local signs (rubor, calor, tumor, dolor) and may also cause systemic manifestations such as fever, leukocytosis, and elevated acute-phase reactants. Tissue injury is generally mild and self-limited if the offending stimulus is eliminated, although severe injury can occur depending on the cause. Therefore, "less prominent local & systemic signs" is not a feature of acute inflammation; this is more characteristic of chronic inflammation, which has a slower onset, mononuclear cell infiltration, and progressive tissue destruction with repair.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Acute inflammation: Rapid onset, short duration, neutrophil predominance.

  • Cardinal signs: Rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa.

  • Systemic features: Fever, leukocytosis, increased CRP/ESR.

  • Chronic inflammation: Lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells, fibrosis, and less dramatic local signs.

Exam Pearl:
Acute inflammation presents with prominent local and systemic manifestations, whereas chronic inflammation is characterized by persistent inflammation, mononuclear cells, and tissue repair/fibrosis.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ৩) Features of hyperemia excludes.......?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Hyperemia is an active process caused by arteriolar dilation, leading to increased blood flow into tissues. The affected tissue becomes red (erythematous) because it is engorged with oxygenated blood. Hyperemia occurs physiologically (e.g., exercising muscle) and pathologically (e.g., acute inflammation). In contrast, congestion is a passive process resulting from impaired venous outflow. Congested tissues appear blue-red (cyanotic) due to the accumulation of deoxygenated blood. Therefore, blue-red color of tissues is a feature of congestion, not hyperemia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hyperemia: Active process due to arteriolar dilation.

  • Hyperemic tissue is bright red because of oxygenated blood.

  • Congestion: Passive process due to impaired venous drainage.

  • Congested tissue appears blue-red (cyanotic) because of deoxygenated blood.

  • Chronic congestion may lead to edema, hypoxia, and hemorrhage.

Exam Pearl:
Hyperemia = Active + arteriolar dilation + oxygenated blood + bright red; Congestion = Passive + venous obstruction + deoxygenated blood + blue-red.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ৪) Which is not one of the three outcomes of acute inflammation?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
The three classic outcomes of acute inflammation are: (1) complete resolution, when the injurious stimulus is eliminated and normal tissue architecture is restored; (2) healing by fibrosis (scarring), when there is substantial tissue destruction or the tissue cannot regenerate; and (3) progression to chronic inflammation, when the injurious agent persists or the acute response fails to eliminate it. Recurrence is not considered one of the standard pathological outcomes of acute inflammation. Although an inflammatory episode may recur clinically if the underlying cause returns, it is not classified as one of the three canonical outcomes.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Three outcomes of acute inflammation:

    • Resolution

    • Healing by fibrosis (scarring)

    • Progression to chronic inflammation

  • Resolution occurs when tissue injury is minimal and regeneration is possible.

  • Fibrosis occurs after extensive tissue damage or in non-regenerating tissues.

  • Persistent injury or infection leads to chronic inflammation.

Exam Pearl:
Remember the three outcomes of acute inflammation: Resolution, Scarring (Fibrosis), and Progression to Chronic Inflammation—Recurrence is not one of them.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ৫) What is the mechanism of oedema in heart failure?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
The edema of heart failure is primarily caused by increased hydrostatic pressure. In congestive heart failure, impaired cardiac pumping leads to elevated venous pressure, which increases capillary hydrostatic pressure and drives fluid from the intravascular space into the interstitial tissues. Right-sided heart failure commonly causes peripheral edema, while left-sided heart failure causes pulmonary edema. Activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) and antidiuretic hormone further promotes sodium and water retention, worsening edema. Increased vascular permeability is typical of inflammation, decreased colloid osmotic pressure occurs in nephrotic syndrome or liver disease, and lymphatic obstruction causes lymphedema.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Heart failure edema is due to increased hydrostatic pressure.

  • Right-sided heart failure: Peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, ascites.

  • Left-sided heart failure: Pulmonary edema.

  • RAAS activation aggravates edema by causing sodium and water retention.

  • Causes of edema:

    • ↑ Hydrostatic pressure – Heart failure

    • ↓ Oncotic pressure – Nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis

    • ↑ Vascular permeability – Inflammation

    • Lymphatic obstruction – Malignancy, filariasis

Exam Pearl:
The hallmark mechanism of edema in congestive heart failure is increased capillary hydrostatic pressure due to elevated venous pressure.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ৬) What type of inflammation occurs in skin blister?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
A skin blister (vesicle or bulla) is a classic example of serous inflammation. It is characterized by the accumulation of protein-poor, cell-poor serous fluid beneath or within the epidermis due to increased vascular permeability. This type of inflammation commonly occurs after minor burns, viral infections, or friction injuries. In contrast, fibrinous inflammation involves fibrin deposition on serosal surfaces (e.g., fibrinous pericarditis), suppurative (purulent) inflammation is characterized by pus formation rich in neutrophils (e.g., abscess), and catarrhal inflammation affects mucous membranes with excessive mucus secretion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Serous inflammation → Blisters, burns, viral vesicles.

  • Fibrinous inflammation → Pericardium, pleura, peritoneum.

  • Suppurative (purulent) inflammation → Abscess, cellulitis, empyema.

  • Catarrhal inflammation → Upper respiratory tract with excessive mucus secretion.

  • Serous exudate contains few inflammatory cells and relatively low protein.

Exam Pearl:
Skin blister = Serous inflammation due to accumulation of serous fluid beneath the epidermis.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ৭) Which are minute (1 to 2 mm in diameter) hemorrhages into skin, mucous membranes, or serosal surfaces?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Petechiae are minute (1–2 mm) pinpoint hemorrhages occurring in the skin, mucous membranes, or serosal surfaces. They commonly result from thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, or increased capillary fragility. Purpura are larger hemorrhages measuring 3–10 mm, while ecchymoses (bruises) are >1–2 cm and are usually caused by trauma or coagulation disorders. The size of the hemorrhage is the key distinguishing feature in examinations.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Petechiae: 1–2 mm pinpoint hemorrhages.

  • Purpura: 3–10 mm hemorrhages.

  • Ecchymoses (bruise): >1–2 cm subcutaneous hemorrhages.

  • Causes of petechiae: Thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, capillary fragility.

  • Ecchymoses undergo color changes due to hemoglobin degradation (red-blue → green → yellow-brown).

Exam Pearl:
Hemorrhage size is highly testable: Petechiae = 1–2 mm, Purpura = 3–10 mm, Ecchymoses = >1–2 cm.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ৮) What is example of suppurative inflammation?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Suppurative (purulent) inflammation is characterized by the production of pus, which consists of neutrophils, necrotic cell debris, edema fluid, and microorganisms. The classic example is an abscess, a localized collection of pus within a tissue caused by pyogenic bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus. Cellulitis is also a suppurative infection, but it is a diffuse spreading inflammation without a localized pus-filled cavity. Skin blister is an example of serous inflammation, and rhinitis is typically catarrhal inflammation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Suppurative (purulent) inflammation = Pus formation with neutrophil predominance.

  • Abscess is the classic example of suppurative inflammation.

  • Common causative organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes.

  • Cellulitis is diffuse suppurative inflammation without a localized cavity.

  • Skin blister → Serous inflammation.

  • Rhinitis → Catarrhal inflammation.

Exam Pearl:
Suppurative inflammation + localized collection of pus = Abscess.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ৯) Thrombi occurring in heart chambers or in the aortic lumen are designated as.......?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Mural thrombi are thrombi that form along the wall of the heart chambers or the lumen of large arteries, especially the aorta. They usually develop in areas of endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), or following myocardial infarction, where damaged endocardium predisposes to thrombosis. Mural thrombi may detach and produce systemic arterial emboli, leading to infarction of organs such as the brain, kidneys, or spleen. In contrast, arterial thrombi generally form within arteries, venous thrombi develop in veins (often the deep veins of the legs), and capillary thrombi are seen in microvascular disorders such as disseminated intravascular coagulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Mural thrombi occur in heart chambers and the aorta.

  • Common causes: Myocardial infarction, dilated cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation.

  • Venous thrombi are rich in red cells and may cause pulmonary embolism.

  • Arterial thrombi are platelet-rich and often develop over atherosclerotic plaques.

  • Virchow's triad: Endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, hypercoagulability.

Exam Pearl:
Heart chamber or aortic wall thrombus = Mural thrombus; it is an important source of systemic arterial emboli.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১০) Plasma protein derived mediators of inflammation excludes?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Inflammatory mediators are broadly classified into plasma protein-derived and cell-derived mediators. Plasma protein-derived mediators are synthesized mainly in the liver and circulate in the plasma as inactive precursors. These include the complement system, kinin system (e.g., bradykinin), and coagulation/fibrinolytic protease systems. In contrast, cytokines (e.g., TNF, IL-1, IL-6) are cell-derived mediators, produced primarily by activated macrophages, lymphocytes, endothelial cells, and other inflammatory cells. Therefore, cytokines are not plasma protein-derived mediators.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Plasma protein-derived mediators:

    • Complement

    • Kinin system (Bradykinin)

    • Coagulation and fibrinolytic proteases

  • Cell-derived mediators:

    • Cytokines (TNF, IL-1, IL-6)

    • Histamine

    • Prostaglandins

    • Leukotrienes

    • Nitric oxide

  • Bradykinin causes pain, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability.

Exam Pearl:
Remember: Complement, kinins, and coagulation/fibrinolytic proteins are plasma-derived; cytokines are cell-derived inflammatory mediators.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১১) Which is not a component of Virchow’s triad of thrombosis?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Virchow's triad describes the three major factors that predispose to thrombosis: (1) endothelial injury, (2) abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), and (3) hypercoagulability. Endothelial injury exposes subendothelial collagen and tissue factor, promoting platelet adhesion and coagulation. Abnormal blood flow disrupts laminar flow and brings platelets into contact with the endothelium. Hypercoagulability may be inherited (e.g., Factor V Leiden mutation) or acquired (e.g., malignancy, pregnancy). Thrombocytosis can increase the risk of thrombosis but is not one of the three components of Virchow's triad.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Virchow's triad:

    • Endothelial injury

    • Abnormal blood flow (stasis/turbulence)

    • Hypercoagulability

  • Stasis is the most important risk factor for venous thrombosis.

  • Endothelial injury is the predominant cause of arterial thrombosis.

  • Hypercoagulability may be inherited or acquired.

Exam Pearl:
Virchow's triad = Endothelial injury + Abnormal blood flow + Hypercoagulability (EAH). Thrombocytosis is not part of the triad.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১২) Which is action of serotonin in inflammation?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) is a vasoactive amine stored mainly in platelet dense granules and released during platelet aggregation. In inflammation, its principal vascular action is vasoconstriction, although its effects may vary depending on the vascular bed and receptor subtype. In contrast, histamine is the major mediator responsible for vasodilation and increased vascular permeability in acute inflammation. Endothelial activation is primarily mediated by cytokines such as TNF and IL-1, rather than serotonin.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Serotonin is released from platelets during platelet activation.

  • Principal action: Vasoconstriction.

  • Histamine causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.

  • TNF and IL-1 mediate endothelial activation.

  • Serotonin is a vasoactive amine, similar to histamine, but with different predominant vascular effects.

Exam Pearl:
In pathology MCQs, remember: Serotonin → Vasoconstriction; Histamine → Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১৩) The vast majority of emboli derive from....?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
The vast majority (more than 99%) of emboli are thromboemboli, arising from dislodged thrombi. These emboli travel through the bloodstream and lodge in distant vessels, causing vascular occlusion and tissue infarction. Venous thromboemboli, usually originating from the deep veins of the lower limbs, commonly cause pulmonary embolism, whereas arterial thromboemboli, often arising from mural thrombi in the left heart or aorta, can produce infarction of the brain, kidneys, spleen, or lower limbs. Fat emboli, air or nitrogen emboli, and atherosclerotic (cholesterol) emboli occur much less frequently.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • >99% of emboli are thromboemboli.

  • Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is the most common source of pulmonary embolism.

  • Left-sided cardiac mural thrombi can cause systemic arterial embolism.

  • Other emboli: Fat, air, amniotic fluid, cholesterol, tumor emboli.

  • Emboli cause ischemia and infarction by obstructing blood flow.

Exam Pearl:
When asked about the most common source of emboli, the answer is almost always: Dislodged thrombus (thromboembolism).

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১৪) Mediators of fever excludes.....?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Fever is primarily mediated by the endogenous pyrogens IL-1 and TNF, which stimulate the production of prostaglandin E₂ (PGE₂) in the hypothalamus. PGE₂ raises the hypothalamic temperature set point, resulting in fever. Therefore, IL-1, TNF, and prostaglandins (especially PGE₂) are key mediators of fever. In contrast, bradykinin is mainly involved in pain, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability during inflammation and is not a principal mediator of fever.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • IL-1 and TNF are endogenous pyrogens.

  • PGE₂ acts on the hypothalamus to produce fever.

  • NSAIDs reduce fever by inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX) and decreasing PGE₂ synthesis.

  • Bradykinin causes pain, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability.

  • IL-6 also contributes to the acute-phase response and fever.

Exam Pearl:
Fever pathway: IL-1/TNF → COX activation → PGE₂ in the hypothalamus → Increased temperature set point. Bradykinin is a mediator of pain, not fever.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১৫) Which leukotriene is required for chemotaxis?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Leukotriene B₄ (LTB₄) is a potent chemotactic agent for neutrophils and other leukocytes. It is produced via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolism and promotes leukocyte recruitment, adhesion to endothelium, activation, and degranulation at sites of inflammation. In contrast, the cysteinyl leukotrienes—LTC₄, LTD₄, and LTE₄—primarily cause bronchoconstriction, vasoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, and mucus secretion, making them important mediators in asthma and allergic reactions.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • LTB₄ → Chemotaxis and activation of neutrophils.

  • LTC₄, LTD₄, LTE₄ → Bronchoconstriction, vasoconstriction, increased vascular permeability.

  • Leukotrienes are synthesized from arachidonic acid via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway.

  • Prostaglandins are produced via the cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway.

Exam Pearl:
Remember: LTB₄ = "B for Bringing neutrophils" (chemotaxis); LTC₄, LTD₄, and LTE₄ = bronchoconstriction and increased vascular permeability.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১৬) Where white infarcts can occur?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
White (anemic) infarcts occur in solid organs with an end-arterial blood supply and limited collateral circulation. The heart, kidney, and spleen are the classic sites. Arterial occlusion in these organs causes coagulative necrosis with little hemorrhage because blood cannot re-enter the infarcted tissue. In contrast, red (hemorrhagic) infarcts occur in tissues with dual blood supply (e.g., lung), loose tissues (e.g., intestine), or after venous occlusion, where blood can seep into the necrotic area.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • White (anemic) infarcts: Heart, kidney, spleen.

  • Occur in solid organs with end-arterial circulation.

  • Histology: Coagulative necrosis (except brain).

  • Red infarcts: Lung, intestine, testis, ovary (especially with venous occlusion or dual blood supply).

  • Brain infarction results in liquefactive necrosis, not coagulative necrosis.

Exam Pearl:
White infarcts occur in solid organs with end-arterial supply—remember: Heart, Kidne

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১৭) In which stage of shock various neurohumoral mechanisms help to maintain cardiac output and blood pressure?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
The initial (non-progressive or compensated) stage of shock is characterized by activation of neurohumoral compensatory mechanisms that help maintain cardiac output and blood pressure despite reduced tissue perfusion. These mechanisms include sympathetic nervous system activation (causing tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction), activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS), and release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Together, they preserve perfusion to vital organs such as the heart and brain. If the underlying cause is not corrected, shock progresses to the progressive stage, followed by the irreversible stage, where severe cellular injury makes recovery unlikely.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Initial (compensated) stage: SNS, RAAS, and ADH maintain BP and cardiac output.

  • Progressive stage: Tissue hypoperfusion → anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acidosis.

  • Irreversible stage: Severe cellular injury with multiorgan failure.

  • Catecholamines increase heart rate and peripheral vasoconstriction during early shock.

Exam Pearl:
Shock is best remembered in three stages: Compensated (neurohumoral compensation) → Progressive (hypoperfusion and acidosis) → Irreversible (multiorgan failure).

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১৮) What type of granuloma is found in leprosy?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Leprosy is characterized by non-caseating granulomatous inflammation, particularly in the tuberculoid form, where a strong cell-mediated immune response leads to well-formed granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans giant cells without central caseous necrosis. In contrast, caseating granulomas are classically seen in tuberculosis, gumma is the granulomatous lesion of tertiary syphilis, and stellate granulomas are characteristic of cat-scratch disease. The term "leprosy" in pathology MCQs generally refers to non-caseating granulomas, although lepromatous leprosy has poorly formed granulomas with numerous bacilli.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Tuberculoid leprosy: Non-caseating granulomas, strong cell-mediated immunity, few bacilli.

  • Lepromatous leprosy: Poorly formed granulomas, numerous bacilli, weak cell-mediated immunity.

  • Caseating granuloma: Tuberculosis.

  • Gumma: Tertiary syphilis.

  • Stellate granuloma: Cat-scratch disease.

Exam Pearl:
Granuloma associations: Tuberculosis → Caseating; Leprosy (tuberculoid) → Non-caseating; Syphilis → Gumma; Cat-scratch disease → Stellate.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ১৯) Which is not a clinical example of cardiogenic shock?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Cardiogenic shock results from failure of the heart to pump effectively, leading to reduced cardiac output despite adequate intravascular volume. Common causes include acute myocardial infarction (MI), severe arrhythmias, and conditions that acutely impair cardiac function. Pulmonary embolism is more accurately classified as obstructive shock, although some older examination questions group it with cardiogenic shock because it causes acute right ventricular failure. Haemorrhage, however, causes hypovolemic shock due to loss of circulating blood volume and is not a cause of cardiogenic shock.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cardiogenic shock: MI, severe arrhythmias, myocarditis, mechanical cardiac complications.

  • Hypovolemic shock: Haemorrhage, severe dehydration, burns.

  • Obstructive shock: Pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax.

  • Septic shock: Distributive shock due to severe infection.

Exam Pearl:
Shock classification is commonly tested: Haemorrhage → Hypovolemic; MI → Cardiogenic; Pulmonary embolism → Obstructive; Sepsis → Distributive.

Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.question: ২০) Which of the following is considered to be permanent tissues according to proliferative capacity?
Inflammation & repair and Hemodynamic Di.exp:
Based on proliferative capacity, tissues are classified as labile, stable, and permanent. Permanent tissues consist of terminally differentiated cells that have lost the ability to undergo mitosis and therefore have minimal regenerative capacity after injury. Cardiac muscle is the classic example of a permanent tissue; damage is repaired by fibrosis (scar formation) rather than regeneration. In contrast, the liver is a stable tissue with remarkable regenerative capacity. The kidney and pancreas also contain predominantly stable cells, which can proliferate to a limited extent after injury.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Labile tissues: Bone marrow, skin, gastrointestinal epithelium.

  • Stable tissues: Liver, kidney, pancreas, fibroblasts, endothelial cells.

  • Permanent tissues: Cardiac muscle, neurons, skeletal muscle (very limited regeneration).

  • Myocardial infarction heals by scar formation, not regeneration.

Exam Pearl:
Remember the classic permanent tissues: Cardiac muscle and neurons—they regenerate poorly and heal by fibrosis.
